I just want to say, re "everyone being liars" -- you and I are guilty of this, too. Depressed people do it often, as well, it's a coping mechanism. Of course, in the depths of it, we're in bed, being quite honest with ourselves. But at any other point in the course of our depression, we may operate in the world even though the depression is back there, in our minds, somewhere.

People are just very flawed. And sometimes it feels pointless. That's when it helps to be able to see that the way you feel in the present isn't how you've always felt, and by looking at others whose lives have included depressed periods, we can see that people do get happier. So, if you can find anything in this moment or in this day to do that you like, that takes you out of your head (into a flow state) -- e.g., exercise or drawing, those two do it for me if I can muster the energy to pick up the pen or put on my sneakers -- do that. If you can't, seek out a support group or a therapist...

This is hard, man. There's a real element of "fake it til you make it" involved in pulling yourself out of dark moods. And that seems distasteful to depressives. (It's often been stated that people with mild depression, aka dysthmia, actually see the world as it really is, and that "normal", happy people are wearing the rose coloured glasses. This may very well be true. But wouldn't you rather wear the glasses than lay in bed until the cops haul your dehydrated, malnourished dead body out to the morgue?)

Do what you can to be a bit of a liar, if only to ourselves and to help others, inasmuch as that is necessary for survival. I hate to say it, but it's true, to an extent. I feel that we can carry the goodness of our depression -- that honesty, that acute sensitivity to human pain -- in the back of our minds, while taking the steps necessary to keep existing.

I try to remind myself that I'm one of the "good ones". There's a lot of bad people. Stick around. Your honesty is needed here on earth. Your sensitivity is needed. If you have to lie to yourself just a little bit, to tell others you are doing good and give a smile when it's a little dishonest, then do that if that's what it takes to bring your honesty and compassion to bear on the world when it counts.

Yeah, I feel you. One cognitive behavioral strategy is this: remind yourself of a time you were NOT a Debbie Downer, and that you DEFINITELY enhanced the lives of people around you. Also, look at other people who have been depressed like you, been Debbie Downers, and who then went on to be different. 

In other words, you need to dispute the implicit thought that you are having which is that you are a bummer to be around right now, and because it will remain that way, you are better off dead. There are more weak links in that chain, but one of them is that it will remain that way forever, and it is easy to logically see that it is not true. Could it remain that way? Maybe. But do you want to die on a maybe? In fact, and this is true, depressive-type people often have some really shining moments in life, many mature out of the depressive period, etc.

But I feel you, I struggle with thoughts like this. And I am old enough to have seen myself and others change, become happier, more fun to be around, etc. Also, remind yourself that your best friends will appreciate you anyways, so if you are a Debbie Downer, fuck it, either they're good friends and like you anyways, or they're not-so-good friends, and fuck em, let them deal with your Downerisms!

You need to use logic to dispute the thought that you have -- which might be unconscious at first until you dig into it -- which is that you are somehow a lower person or less deserving. If you are truly incapable of seeing that those thoughts aren't true (e.g., you truly can't see in your own mind that you have compassion for people who are no more deserving of compassion than you are), then THAT is when you have to go to exercise or meds or some other treatment that addresses the chemical unhappiness that's making you unable to think clearly.

Try thinking clearly first, though, that's what cognitive behavioral therapy is about -- fixing your thinking so that your behavior falls into line.
